clue.text: Articles about wearing suit in camp

parts.note: THE and A are the definite and indefinite articles

indicators.note: the short word for about is worn inside the word for a lawsuit

parts.note: a suit at law is a trial
C is short for circa, about

explanation.surface: Something about articles of clothing worn with a suit at a holiday camp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wearing' puts C inside TRIAL. 'Camp' is the definition in its sense of showy and affected, not a place to stay.
explanation.definitionFit: Camp behaviour is exaggerated and stagey, which is a synonym for over-dramatic in manner.

clue.text: Rule for each individual framed by one parent

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one is I

indicators.note: the words for each and individual sit inside the word for parent, like a picture in a frame

parts.note: mum is a mother, a parent
per means for each, as in per head
I is a single person, an individual

explanation.surface: A household rule set for each child, laid down by one parent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'framed by' puts PERI inside MUM, after the I for 'one'.
explanation.definitionFit: Imperium is the Latin word for supreme power or command, that is, authority to govern.

clue.text: Puzzle's meaning can be decoded without a name

indicators.note: decoding scrambled letters means rearranging them into sense, so this signals reshuffling
without means the letter for name is dropped from the word

explanation.surface: A puzzle's hidden meaning can be worked out even without a name to go on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' takes N out of MEANING to leave MEAING, and 'can be decoded' rearranges that.
explanation.definitionFit: An enigma is a mystery or riddle, something baffling; the famous German cipher machine shared the name.

clue.text: Landowner doesn't finish hideout

indicators.note: the word stops short, losing its last letter

parts.note: a laird is a Scottish landowner

explanation.surface: A landowner leaves his hideout unfinished.
explanation.walkthrough: A LAIRD is a Scottish estate owner; 'doesn't finish' cuts the final D.
explanation.definitionFit: A lair is an animal's den, and by extension any secret hiding place.

clue.text: Decide moves after Woman's Own's first brave feat

indicators.note: the scrambled part comes after the rest

parts.note: her is the possessive for a woman

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the word Own is used
the letters of Decide move around into a new order

explanation.surface: A magazine, Woman's Own, decides to run a piece on someone's brave feat.
explanation.walkthrough: Woman's Own is a long-running British women's weekly magazine. Its title is split: 'Woman's' and 'Own's first' work separately, and 'moves' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A heroic deed is a courageous act, matching a brave feat word for word.

clue.text: Latin repetition not working for bookworms

indicators.note: working is ON, so not working removes those two letters

parts.note: iteration is repetition

explanation.surface: Bookworms find endlessly repeating Latin is not working for them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not working' strips ON (working, as a machine is on) from ITERATION, leaving ITERATI.
explanation.definitionFit: The literati are well-read, literary people, the educated class devoted to books.

clue.text: Saw one in Glasgow filling sink

indicators.note: the Scots word for one goes inside the word for sink

parts.note: to sag is to sink or droop
yin is the Scots word for one

explanation.surface: Someone in Glasgow saw a man filling a sink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' looks like the past of see; it is the noun, an old saying. YIN is Scots for one.
explanation.definitionFit: A saw is a proverb or maxim, and so is a saying.

clue.text: Innocent, maybe: a thousand and eleven fled Pompeii

indicators.note: these letters leave the town's name, as its people fled

parts.note: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand
eleven read as one-one, two Roman I's

explanation.surface: An innocent fled Pompeii along with a thousand and eleven others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Innocent' looks like an adjective but is a papal name; thirteen popes took it. 'fled' removes M and II from POMPEII.
explanation.definitionFit: Innocent was the name of several popes, so it is an example of a pontiff, signalled by 'maybe'.

clue.text: All of us sniff a new career

parts.note: hum is slang for a smell, as is a sniff
to career is to rush along, to race

explanation.surface: All of us would turn our noses up at a new career.
explanation.walkthrough: 'career' is a verb here, to hurtle, not a profession.
explanation.definitionFit: Humankind as a whole includes every person, so the phrase covers everyone, all of us.

clue.text: I love tackling journal's final stage of development

indicators.note: the zero for love comes up behind the journal, attacking it from the rear

parts.note: a mag is a magazine, a journal
love is zero in tennis, O

explanation.surface: Someone who loves taking on a journal's final stage of development.
explanation.definitionFit: An imago is the adult insect, the last phase of metamorphosis after the larva and pupa.

clue.text: Agent of retribution, English, lying in state

indicators.note: the abbreviation for English lies inside the verb for state

parts.note: to aver is to state firmly

explanation.surface: An English agent of retribution lies in state after death.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lying in state' suggests a funeral, but 'state' is the verb to declare.
explanation.definitionFit: An avenger is someone who exacts vengeance, inflicting punishment for a wrong.

clue.text: Former duck trap that is snaring mallard's head

parts.note: a duck is zero in cricket, O
a net traps fish or birds

indicators.note: the Latin abbreviation for that is catches the bird's first letter

parts.note: ie is the abbreviation of id est, that is

indicators.note: the head of the word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A former duck trap, the kind that snared a mallard by its head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'duck' is the cricket score of nought, O, not the bird, though mallard sits beside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Onetime is an adjective meaning former or erstwhile, as in a onetime champion.

clue.text: Educated girl eating a yogurt dish

indicators.note: the girl's name takes in the letter A

parts.note: Rita is the heroine of the play and film Educating Rita

explanation.surface: A well-schooled girl eats a yogurt dish.
explanation.walkthrough: Educating Rita is Willy Russell's play about a hairdresser who studies literature, so the educated girl is RITA.
explanation.definitionFit: Raita is an Indian side dish of yogurt with cucumber or mint.

clue.text: American ready to separate opposing sides in port

indicators.note: the money word goes between right and left, keeping them apart

parts.note: right and left, R and L, are opposite sides
ready is slang for cash, which is also change

explanation.surface: An American ready to step between two warring sides in a port.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ready' means money (the readies), not prepared.
explanation.definitionFit: Archangel, or Arkhangelsk, is a seaport in northern Russia on the White Sea.

clue.text: Extra maths problem starts to annoy lazybones

parts.note: an addition is a sum, a maths problem

indicators.note: the opening letters of the next two words

explanation.surface: An extra maths problem set to annoy a lazy pupil.
explanation.definitionFit: Additional means further or supplementary, a synonym of extra.

clue.text: Not how Ko-Ko operates, lacking spirit

definitions.meaning: Ko-Ko, the executioner in Gilbert and Sullivan's The Mikado, sings 'I've got a little list' of victims, so he works with a list

explanation.surface: An executioner going about his work without much enthusiasm.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the first half as list-less-ly: without a list, unlike Ko-Ko.
explanation.definitionFit: Listless means languid and lacking energy, so doing something that way is spiritless.

clue.text: Smiley's group jams here in central London?

definitions.meaning: in John le Carré's spy novels George Smiley works for the Circus, the secret service, headquartered at this junction
a busy road junction in London's West End where traffic jams

explanation.surface: A spy's team causes traffic jams in central London.
explanation.walkthrough: Cambridge Circus is a busy junction at Charing Cross Road and Shaftesbury Avenue; le Carré's spies call their HQ there 'the Circus'.
explanation.definitionFit: The same London place names both the fictional spy headquarters and a congested road junction.

clue.text: Clear fingerprint impressed into actual tablet

indicators.note: the fingerprint word is pressed inside the word for actual

parts.note: real means actual
a dab is slang for a fingerprint
E is slang for an ecstasy tablet

explanation.surface: A clear fingerprint has been pressed into an actual stone tablet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tablet' is a drug pill, the ecstasy E, not a writing slab.
explanation.definitionFit: Clear writing is legible, easy to make out and follow.

clue.text: College on lookout to host large assembly

indicators.note: the lookout word takes in the letter for large as a guest

parts.note: cave, Latin for beware, was the schoolboy cry of a lookout
L is the size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: A college on the lookout for somewhere to host a large assembly.
explanation.walkthrough: CAVE (two syllables, 'kay-vee') was the warning a British public schoolboy on lookout shouted.
explanation.definitionFit: A conclave is a private meeting, notably the gathering of cardinals that elects a pope.

clue.text: Carpeted stable dam wrecked

indicators.note: wrecking the words breaks them up so the letters can be rebuilt

explanation.surface: A floor in a wrecked stable, dam laid with carpet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carpeted' looks like floor covering; it means reprimanded.
explanation.definitionFit: To be carpeted is to be hauled up and scolded; lambasted means harshly criticised.

clue.text: State capital needs a good deal to secure province

indicators.note: the quantity word closes around the province's letters

parts.note: much means a good deal
NI is Northern Ireland, often called the Province

explanation.surface: A state capital needing a good deal of money to keep hold of a province.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface recalls the 1938 Munich agreement over the Sudetenland.
explanation.definitionFit: Munich is the capital city of Bavaria, a German federal state.

clue.text: Tin and aluminium locks here

parts.note: a can is a tin
Al is the chemical symbol for aluminium

explanation.surface: Tin and aluminium are used to make locks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'locks' looks like door fittings; they are the gates on a waterway.
explanation.definitionFit: Waterways have locks that raise and lower boats, so a navigation is where they are found.

clue.text: Clubs and diamonds run out for consul

parts.note: C is the card suit abbreviation for clubs
ice is slang for diamonds
R is the cricket abbreviation for run
O stands for out

explanation.surface: A card player's clubs and diamonds run out, leaving the consul short.
explanation.walkthrough: 'diamonds' looks like the card suit after 'Clubs'; it is gems, slang ICE.
explanation.definitionFit: Cicero was a Roman statesman and orator who served as consul in 63 BC.

clue.text: Note silence among ladies in bygone times

indicators.note: the note and silence words go among the letters of the toilet word

parts.note: the ladies is a women's toilet, a loo
to gag is to silence

explanation.surface: Remembering a note of silence among ladies in bygone times.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an adverb meaning in the distant past, as is in bygone times.

clue.text: Port given permission to entertain foreign leader

indicators.note: the permission word takes in a guest letter

parts.note: let means allow, give permission

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A port given permission to welcome a foreign leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' looks like a harbour; it is the left side of a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Port is the nautical term for the side of a vessel on your left facing forward.

clue.text: Journos, gathering in loose ends, raise them in anger

indicators.note: the journalists word collects letters inside it

parts.note: hacks are journalists

indicators.note: the two ends of the word, its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Reporters scooping up loose ends, which raise tempers.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a phrase: something you raise when angry, as in raising your hackles.
explanation.definitionFit: Hackles are neck hairs raised by an angry animal; raising them is an idiom for becoming angry.

clue.text: Ambassador and bishop's address in 20

definitions.note: a form of address in the city at 20 down, a German city

parts.note: HE, His Excellency, is the title of an ambassador
RR, Right Reverend, is a bishop's title

explanation.surface: How an ambassador and a bishop are addressed in a state capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 20 is the German city, so the address is German for Mr.
explanation.definitionFit: Herr is the German courtesy title for a man, equivalent to Mister.

clue.text: Centre Point's fine old state

definitions.note: possessive phrase standing for an adjective, relating to the centre point

parts.note: F is the pencil-grading abbreviation for fine
Cal is short for California, a US state

explanation.surface: Centre Point, London's office tower, is a fine old building in good shape.
explanation.walkthrough: Centre Point is a 1960s tower block in central London; here it is just the centre point, or focus.
explanation.definitionFit: Focal means relating to a focus, the central point where things meet.

clue.text: Song by East End barman is going places fast

parts.note: an air is a tune or song

indicators.note: the end of the word is its last letter

parts.note: Ravel, a composer, writes bars of music, so a bar man

explanation.surface: A Cockney barman's song as he goes places fast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'East End' suggests London's Cockneys, but 'End' takes the last letter of East. Maurice Ravel, composer of Bolero, is jokily a 'barman'.
explanation.definitionFit: Flying is a quick way of journeying, so travel by aeroplane is getting places fast.
